newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Wallis not likely to trouble Westpac's bid.
newsitem.headline: Wallis not likely to trouble Westpac's bid.

text.p: The upcoming Wallis report into Australia's financial system would not represent a stumbling block for Westpac Banking Corp's plan to takeover Bank of Melbourne Ltd, political and industry analysts said.
If anything, the Wallis report was likely to redefine the market in a way that would promote further rationalisation in the financial services industry.
A Sydney-based banking analyst, who asked not to be named, said the report was expected to widen the definition of the financial sector beyond the banks and major life insurance companies.

"The ACCC (Australian Competition and Consumer Commission) and (chairman) Allan Fels have been concentrating on the banks as special institutions in a market within themselves rather than part of a wider financial services market," the analyst said.
"(The widening of that definition) will provide scope for further rationalisation at the lower end."

The Wallis report, which was due for release sometime next week, was expected to include a recommendation to end the current "six pillars" policy which prevented mergers between the four big Australian banks (including Westpac) and the two largest life offices.
It was also expected to leave the powers of the ACCC untouched, making the regulatory watchdog and Treasurer Peter Costello the main obstacles to the A$1.435 billion takeover.

Analysts said they did not expect the report to cause Costello to use his powers under banking legislation to veto the bid, meaning the spotlight would remain on the ACCC and its attitude towards bank mergers.
However, analysts said a large degree of uncertainty about the impact of the report remained in the market, particularly as Costello has stressed that he need not accept any of its recommendations.

"The whole situation, I think, is still fairly fluid in terms of what actually comes out of this Wallis inquiry but whatever comes out of it, I would be extremely surprised if anything is done to actually usurp the powers of the ACCC," a Brisbane-based analyst said.
"So I still think the whole thing is going to hold constant."
The ACCC has said previously it would not approve mergers that removed the last regional bank from a state market, a stipulation which may apply to the Bank of Melbourne.

But the merger plan was for the two banks to merge the retail operations in Victoria and keep the Bank of Melbourne name. Regional banks are characterised by a loan book that is heavily tilted towards mortgages and small-medium sized business lending.
"The ACCC is the only problem -- I don't think the Wallis inquiry is much of an issue at all," said Austock Brokers research director David Perry.
"My guess is that there's probably a 50 or 60 percent probability of the merger getting up, although no one really believes the Wallis inquiry is going to change the ground rules for this situation."
The inquiry, set up by the government and headed by former Amcor Ltd chief executive Stan Wallis, is the first major review of Australian finance sector regulations since the early 1980s.
